- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.40), model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid excessive pessimism.  
- After a sharp price spike, model often overshoots and fails to correct — reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and add a slight downward slope to avoid overreaction.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mildly positive (e.g., 0.0 to +0.30), model frequently underestimates upward momentum — increase forecast by 2–5% for the next 3–5 days.  
- Model consistently underestimates mean reversion in the short term (1–3 days) — add a small upward bias (1–3%) if sentiment is neutral or slightly negative.  
- For 30-day forecasts, model often fails to capture long-term trend shifts — if sentiment turns positive after 10–15 days, increase forecast by 3–5% to reflect momentum.  
- When sentiment is consistently negative over 5+ days, model tends to ignore underlying support — add a floor at 5–10% below recent low to prevent collapse.  
- If sentiment is positive but volatile (e.g., alternating +0.1 to -0.2), model overfits noise — smooth forecast by averaging last 3–5 days’ values before applying sentiment-weighted adjustment.
